newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish fund manager warns of high share prices.
newsitem.headline: Swedish fund manager warns of high share prices.

text.p: High Swedish share prices do not reflect the new business climate of low inflation and downward price pressure on products, the head of a major pension fund said on Thursday.

"Worldwide development...with no inflation to speak of, with a high savings ratio and thereby weak consumption, is likely to gradually increase competition on most goods and service markets," Fourth AP fund chief Thomas Halvorsen said in the fund's annual report.
"This in turn will lead to worsened margins and lower profitability in the business community," he wrote.
Halvorsen is one of the largest fund managers on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, with a portfolio which has grown to close to 70 billion crowns from 25 billion in 1992.
Over the past five years the fund's capital has risen by 23 percent annually and in the decade since 1987 it has gained an average 18 percent per year.
"Such a high return over such a long period of time calls for careful consideration," he said. "Average risk-free interest rates were not close to these figures during the period."
Halvorsen recalled that the bourse was at high levels in 1986 and early 1987, before its collapse later in the year.
Although much indicates that share prices are on firmer ground now than 10 years ago, he expected margin squeezes and lower profitability in the long term.
"It would be surprising, at least for me, if companies long term manage to have a return on capital much above investors' required return," Halvorsen said.
